title: Ready for Outside
tagline: Look, listen, and help Pip choose for today.
learningGoal: Use visible weather and a spoken temperature clue to choose an item that helps with a specific outdoor task.
childTakeaway: I look at the weather and choose something that helps.
story: Pip wants a short walk to the park bench. The same park feels different as weather changes, so Pip needs help choosing useful clothing and equipment.
introPip: I’m going outside! Look at the weather with me. We can choose something that helps for today.
conceptImageAlt: Pip, a smiling silver-gray ball with blue seams, sits on a dry porch beside a blue umbrella, green hooded raincoat, and yellow brimmed hat. Gentle rain falls over a leafy park and bench outside.

ageSupport.entry: Offer two choices, name both aloud, and model looking at the sky. State cold or warm in speech; do not expect the child to read weather symbols.
ageSupport.stretch: Ask the child to explain a useful choice, then notice that the same place can need a different item after weather changes. Round five accepts either of two sensible choices.

misconception: A sunny sky always means the air is warm, or there is only one correct outfit for every kind of weather.

rounds.title: A roof for the rain
rounds.prompt: It is raining. Pip wants to open a wide cover and hold it above him. Which item can do that?
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip in a park with visible falling raindrops and a puddle. Below are a brimmed hat on the left and an open umbrella on the right.
rounds.success: The open umbrella makes a wide cover above Pip. Falling rain hits the cover.
hints: Look at the falling drops. Pip wants a cover that opens above him.
Imagine each item opened or worn. Which makes a wide roof above Pip?
The umbrella opens into a wide cover. Hold it above Pip to catch the falling drops.
rounds.visualHint: Place the umbrella above Pip, then animate drops hitting its canopy. No cue is present before the hint.
rounds.whyThisRound: An easy functional match between visible rain and an opening overhead cover; the task wording distinguishes the umbrella from the rigid pictured hat.

rounds.title: A warmer layer
rounds.prompt: It is cold and dry today. Which layer could help Pip feel warmer outside?
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip in a dry cloudy park. Below are shorts on the left, a toy ball in the middle, and a warm coat on the right.
rounds.success: A warm coat adds a layer around Pip. That layer can help him feel warmer in the cold air.
hints: Listen to the weather clue: it is cold. Pip needs a warmer layer.
Look for clothing that covers much of the body. The ball is for playing.
The warm coat covers the body and adds a warm layer. Shorts cover much less.
rounds.visualHint: Show the coat wrapping around a neutral mannequin beside Pip, then compare how much body it covers with the shorts.
rounds.whyThisRound: Transfers from keeping rain off to adding warmth. The spoken temperature clue supplies information that a cloudy sky alone cannot give.

rounds.title: Sunshine can be cold
rounds.prompt: The sun is shining, but the air is cold. Which layer could help Pip feel warmer?
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip in the same park with a visible sun and small patches of snow on the ground. Below are a warm coat on the left, a thin short-sleeved shirt in the middle, and an umbrella on the right.
rounds.success: The coat adds a warmer layer. Sunshine and cold air can happen together, so we listen to how the air feels too.
hints: We can see sunshine. What did Pip say about the air?
Pip said the air is cold. Think about a layer that covers his body and helps keep warmth close.
Choose the warm coat for the cold air. A sunny sky does not tell us the air is warm.
rounds.visualHint: Replay the words “the air is cold,” then compare the coat and shirt coverage. Keep the sun visible throughout.
rounds.whyThisRound: Reveals the misconception that sunshine always means warm weather without asking children to read a thermometer.

rounds.title: Shade for a face
rounds.prompt: The sun is shining. Pip wants shade over his face while he walks. Which item helps?
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip in a sunny park beside the bench and tree. Below are a boot on the left, a broad-brimmed hat in the middle, and a warm coat on the right.
rounds.success: The hat’s brim sticks out over Pip’s face and makes some shade there.
hints: Pip wants shade on his face. Look for something worn above the face.
Imagine wearing each item. Which has a part that sticks out over the eyes?
The brimmed hat has a wide edge. That edge can make shade on Pip’s face.
rounds.visualHint: Place the hat on Pip and show a simple face-shadow patch beneath the brim. Explain partial shade only.
rounds.whyThisRound: Transfer to a clearly stated sun-related task. It asks about making shade, not inferring temperature or providing complete sun protection.

rounds.title: Two sensible rain helpers
rounds.prompt: Rain has started in this same park. Pip wants to keep falling rain off his clothes. Choose one item that could help.
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip beside the same bench and tree as the previous round, now under rain clouds with falling drops and a puddle. Below are a hooded raincoat on the left, a brimmed hat in the middle, and an umbrella on the right.
rounds.success: A raincoat covers clothes; an umbrella makes a cover above them. Either can help with this gentle falling rain. You can choose one.
hints: The place is the same, but the weather has changed. What is falling from the clouds?
Pip wants to cover his clothes. A cover can be worn around them or held above them.
A raincoat covers clothes, and an umbrella catches rain above them. Both are sensible choices here. Choose either one.
rounds.visualHint: After the choice, offer a demonstration of either strategy: drops hit the raincoat, or drops hit the umbrella overhead. Never require selecting both.
rounds.whyThisRound: An optional stretch checks a changed weather condition and accepts two reasonable solutions to the same functional task.

finale: Pip checks the weather again, chooses a useful item, and reaches the park bench ready for the short walk. The child can explain one choice in words or by pointing.
offlineActivity: With a grown-up, look through a window and name what you can see. Have the grown-up say whether the air feels cold or warm, then choose one useful item for a planned short outing and explain what it helps with.
reviewQuestions: Does “which item helps with this task?” feel more inviting than testing a single correct outfit, and is the task understandable without reading?
Should the sunny-but-cold example stay in the core five rounds, or become an optional stretch for children who are ready?
In the last round, should we show both sensible rain strategies after one selection, or let the child request the second demonstration?
designNotes: Adult review concept only; no game integration, voice service calls, child testing, or curriculum validation has occurred.
Spoken weather conditions are part of the stimulus: sunshine alone does not establish temperature, and clouds alone do not establish cold.
Question scenes have no answer-revealing highlights, arrows, checkmarks, or selected styling. Choice order changes.
Pip is a fantasy ball character; garment demonstrations would need a simple mannequin or clear symbolic dressing interaction, not a claim about ball anatomy.
The functional task narrows each choice. Accept culturally reasonable clothing alternatives in a future implementation rather than treating one pictured outfit as universal.
Round five accepts raincoat OR umbrella as an individual answer. It is not a hidden multi-select task. The brimmed hat alone does not cover Pip’s clothes as requested.
Hat feedback describes partial face shade. This pack does not present any one item as complete sun protection or offer medical advice.
Gentle ordinary weather is used. Severe-weather safety, wind-driven rain, weather forecasting, temperature reading, and cloud taxonomy are outside this short lesson.
The NOAA source supports observing separate weather features and noticing change; it does not validate this preschool lesson or prescribe particular outfits.

sources.title: NOAA: Be a Citizen Weather Reporter
sources.supports: Weather observations include temperature, precipitation, and sky conditions as separate features. Repeated observations reveal changes over time; adapted here into looking and listening before choosing a useful item.
